query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, stress–strain behavior, thermal expansion, and elastic behavior at elevated temperatures remain insufficiently understood. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain these responses? Define a controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline state, the temperature and response limits within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, thermally induced lattice distortions in single‐phase BCC HfNbTaTiZr cause a transition from a nearly isotropic elastic state at room temperature to increased elastic anisotropy. This drives heterogeneous load sharing among grains and promotes enhanced edge dislocation activity, which together yield a plateau in yield strength and a measurable change in the thermal expansion behavior relative to the room‐temperature baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy in its homogeneous, single-phase BCC solid-solution state with near isotropic elastic response at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Conducting controlled tensile, creep (nanoindentation), and thermal expansion tests on HfNbTaTiZr samples at elevated temperatures (e.g., 673 K to 1073 K) compared with baseline room temperature measurements.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under static and low strain-rate conditions at room temperature (baseline) and then at elevated temperatures between approximately 673 K and 1073 K to capture any transitions in elastic and plastic responses.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced lattice distortions that increase elastic anisotropy at the grain level, altering the distribution of local stresses and activating edge dislocation slip.
generation.mechanism: As temperature rises, anharmonic lattice vibrations and thermal expansion introduce distortions that break the uniform (isotropic) load-sharing seen at room temperature. This increased elastic anisotropy leads to heterogeneous stress distributions among grains that facilitate edge dislocation motion. The edge dislocations, encountering higher energy barriers for glide, help maintain yield strength (forming a plateau) even as overall stiffness reduces, and modulate the thermal expansion response.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the room temperature baseline, at elevated temperatures (673–1073 K) the alloy will exhibit (1) a nearly constant yield strength (a plateau) despite reduced stiffness, (2) a higher and more variable elastic modulus among different grain orientations, and (3) an increased thermal expansion coefficient consistent with enhanced lattice anharmonicity.
generation.baseline: Measurements of stress–strain behavior, elastic moduli, and thermal expansion performed at room temperature, where the alloy shows nearly isotropic elastic response and uniform dislocation activation.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to hold within the temperature range from about 673 K to 1073 K; outside this range (at lower cryogenic temperatures or near melting/phase-transition temperatures) different mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the anisotropy increase and its direct correlation to edge dislocation density and activity are not fully established; detailed microstructural studies (e.g., neutron diffraction and TEM) are needed to refine these correlations.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ tensile and nanoindentation creep tests and thermal expansion measurements on HfNbTaTiZr samples at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (673–1073 K). Use neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM to monitor grain-specific elastic moduli and dislocation activity during loading.
measurements: Elastic moduli for various crystallographic orientations
Dislocation density and edge dislocation activity via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant increase in elastic anisotropy or corresponding variations in grain-level moduli are observed at elevated temperatures, and if the yield strength does not exhibit a plateau (i.e., it declines continuously as temperature increases), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: To demonstrate these predicted unusual deformation behaviors, we investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behavior for the NbTaTiV BCC refractory HEA at RT and elevated temperatures, using in situ neutron experiments and theoretical approaches. Different from the conventional BCC alloys (), the lattice strain evolution and measured diffraction elastic moduli indicate the elastically isotropic behavior at RT. The magnitudes of single-crystal and macroscopic elastic moduli, obtained by in situ neutron experiments and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS), respectively, are compared to theoretical calculations, including first-principles calculations and machine learning (ML) approaches. Furthermore, it is found that the present NbTaTiV refractory HEA indicates the lack of strong temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior at elevated temperatures, which is atypical elastic deformation behavior, compared to other conventional metallic materials ().

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

In service, one of the essential design criteria for engineering components is the time-dependent deformation behavior (i.e., creep resistance). Macroscopic bulk compression or tension [,,], micro-pillar compression [,], and nano-indentation technique [,,,,,,] have been used to investigate the deformation behavior of materials in a wide range of length scales. Major discrepancies between the data obtained by nano-indentation and via conventional creep testing (i.e., compression/tension) have been reported [,]. This may be due to the complex multi-axial and inhomogeneous stress below indenters in comparison with uniaxial and homogeneous stress during bulk compression/tension test []. Despite these discrepancies, nano-indentation has been used as a convenient and fast approach to characterize the time-dependent deformation behavior at the small-scale for pure metals [,], bulk metallic glasses [,], and HEAs [,,,,,,,]. Most nano-indentation creep studies are limited to room temperature, low load (<100 mN), and face-centered cubic (FCC) metals/alloys [,,,,,,].
